entries.title: Place value and changing bases
headings: The idea: a digit counts bundles
Reading a numeral: base b to decimal
Worked examples: base b to decimal
Writing a number in base b: repeated division
Worked examples: decimal to base b
How many digits does a number need?
When the base is the unknown
entries.text: Every number a digital system stores is a row of digits, and every digit means how many of something. In this lesson you learn to read a numeral in any base, to write any number in any base, to move between bases, to count how many digits a number needs, and to solve the GATE puzzles where the base itself is the unknown. By the end, a question like "for which base b is (312)_b \div (20)_b = (13.1)_b?" will be a two-minute calculation, not a guess. Where this fits This is the first lesson of Digital Logic, and almost everything later leans on it. Binary, octal and hexadecimal (next lesson) are just bases 2, 8 and 16. Fractions and fixed point (Lesson 3) extend place value to the right of the point. Signed numbers (Lesson 4) reuse the same digits with one place given a negative weight. Later chapters read counter states, memory addresses and IEEE-754 fields with exactly the tools built here. The idea: a digit counts bundles Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets (9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate (27), then two boxes (18), no packets, and one loose item. The record reads 1 2 0 1. Each position holds the number of bundles of one size, and the sizes grow by the same factor (here 3) as you move left. A position can never hold 3 or more, because three of anything would be packed into one bundle of the next size. That one rule, "pack as soon as you reach the base", is all of positional notation. Our everyday decimal is the same shop with bundles of ten. An odometer is the same shop in motion. Watch a counter whose wheels only know the digits 0, 1 and 2: when a wheel would reach 3 it rolls back to 0 and nudges its neighbour forward. Notice what the counter shows after three counts: 10. In base 3, "10" means one bundle of three and nothing loose, which is three. That is why "10" means the base itself in every base: ten in decimal, two in binary, sixteen in hexadecimal. Fix a whole number b \ge 2, the base (also called the radix). A base-b numeral is a string of digits d_k d_{k-1} \dots d_1 d_0, optionally followed by a radix point and more digits d_{-1} d_{-2} \dots, where every digit satisfies 0 \le d_i \le b-1. Its value is (d_k \dots d_1 d_0 . d_{-1} d_{-2} \dots)_b \;=\; \sum_i d_i \, b^{\,i}. d_i is the digit in position i, counted from 0 just left of the point. b^{\,i} is the place value (weight) of position i: \dots, b^2, b, 1, b^{-1}, b^{-2}, \dots Digits ten to thirty-five are written A to Z, so in hexadecimal A = 10, B = 11, …, F = 15. The subscript names the base: (1201)_3, (2D)_{16}. A numeral with no subscript is decimal. Here is that definition doing its work: the same four digits, first read in base 3 and then in base 5. Only the place values change. In base b the only digits are 0, 1, \dots, b-1. A numeral that contains a digit d is a valid base-b numeral only when b > d, so the base is at least one more than the largest digit. For example (4072)_b forces b \ge 8, and (19)_8 is not an octal numeral at all. Why insist on this? Two reasons, and both matter for GATE. First, a digit equal to b or more would be a full bundle that should have been carried into the next place, so allowing it would let one number have several spellings ((13)_2 would equal (101)_2). Second, in every "find the base" question the digit limit is the condition that throws away fake solutions. The equation alone is never the whole question. Which of these are valid numerals? (3021)_3, (777)_8, (1G)_{16}, (10)_2. (777)_8 and (10)_2 are valid. (3021)_3 uses the digit 3, which needs base 4 or more. (1G)_{16} uses G = 16, which needs base 17 or more. A digit says how many bundles; its position says which bundle size, b^{\,i}. Every digit is at most b-1, so the base exceeds the largest digit. "10" in base b is b itself. Reading a numeral: base b to decimal To find the value of a numeral, you simply add up digit × place value. There are two ways to organise that sum, and you should be fluent in both. Expansion. By the definition, a numeral with digits d_k \dots d_0 is worth N = d_k b^k + d_{k-1} b^{k-1} + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 . Horner's form. Every term except the last has a factor b, so take it out. Inside the bracket every term except the last again has a factor b; take it out again, and repeat: \begin{aligned} N &= \big(d_k b^{k-1} + d_{k-1} b^{k-2} + \dots + d_1\big)\, b + d_0 \\ &= \Big(\big(d_k b^{k-2} + \dots + d_2\big)\, b + d_1\Big)\, b + d_0 \\ &= \Big(\dots\big((d_k\, b + d_{k-1})\, b + d_{k-2}\big)\, b + \dots\Big)\, b + d_0 . \end{aligned} So you can read a numeral left to right with a single running total t: start with t = 0 and, for each digit d, replace t by t \cdot b + d. After the last digit, t = N. Sanity check. For (1201)_3 the expansion gives 27 + 18 + 0 + 1 = 46, and the chain gives 0 \to 1 \to 1\cdot 3 + 2 = 5 \to 5 \cdot 3 + 0 = 15 \to 15 \cdot 3 + 1 = 46. The two forms agree, as they must, because they are the same sum with the brackets moved. Fraction digits. A digit d_{-j} after the point is worth d_{-j}\, b^{-j}, so (0.8)_{16} = 8/16 = 0.5 and (0.101)_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac18 = 0.625. Keep one running total. For each digit, multiply the total by the base and add the digit. For (11010)_2: 1 \to 3 \to 6 \to 13 \to 26. Why it works: it is the bracketed form from the derivation, evaluated from the inside out. When it fails: never for whole numbers. For fraction digits it does not apply directly; read those by place value (or run Horner on the digits and divide by b^{\,f}, where f is the number of fraction digits). Worked examples: base b to decimal Find the decimal value of (11010)_2. Write the place values under the digits, starting with 2^0 = 1 on the right. \begin{array}{ccccc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 16 & 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} Add the place values that sit under a 1: 16 + 8 + 2 = 26. Check with Horner: 1 \to 2\cdot1+1 = 3 \to 2\cdot3+0 = 6 \to 2\cdot6+1 = 13 \to 2\cdot13+0 = 26.

entries.title: Place value and changing bases
headings: Reading a number in any base
Why every number has one spelling
entries.text: A digit's value depends on where it sits. That one idea, place value, is all you need to read a number written in any base. The big idea Pay ₹347 with notes and coins: 3 hundred-rupee notes, 4 tens, 7 ones. The digit says how many; the position says of what size. Base 2 works the same way, only the bundles are 1, 2, 4, 8, … instead of 1, 10, 100. In base b, the digit in position i (counting from 0 on the right) is worth d_i \cdot b^{\,i}. Every digit must satisfy 0 \le d_i < b. Radix is another word for base. GATE papers use both. Reading a number in any base Add up digit × place value over every position: N = d_k b^k + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 = \sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\, b^{\,i} Factor out b again and again and the same sum becomes a chain of "multiply, then add": N = \big( \dots ( d_k\, b + d_{k-1} )\, b + \dots \big)\, b + d_0 Convert (1011)_2 to decimal. Write the place value under each digit. \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2^3 & 2^2 & 2^1 & 2^0 \\ 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} Multiply each digit by its place value. \begin{aligned} 1 \cdot 8 &= 8 \\ 0 \cdot 4 &= 0 \\ 1 \cdot 2 &= 2 \\ 1 \cdot 1 &= 1 \end{aligned} Add the contributions: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. (1011)_2 = 11 Convert (257)_8 to decimal. List the place values from the right: 1, 8, 64. Weight each digit. \begin{aligned} 2 \cdot 64 &= 128 \\ 5 \cdot 8 &= 40 \\ 7 \cdot 1 &= 7 \end{aligned} Add: 128 + 40 + 7 = 175. (257)_8 = 175 For which base b is (31)_b = 16? Expand the left side: (31)_b = 3 \cdot b + 1. Solve 3b + 1 = 16, which gives b = 5. Check the digits: 3 < 5 and 1 < 5, so (31)_5 is a valid numeral. b = 5 Why every number has one spelling Every whole number N \ge 0 has exactly one numeral in base b without leading zeros. The last digit is forced: every other term is a multiple of b, so d_0 is the remainder of N \div b. Remove it, divide by b, and the next digit is forced the same way. Repeat until nothing is left. Since no step had a choice, no two numerals can share a value. What is (110)_2 in decimal? 1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 1 = 6. Read binary left to right in your head: start at 0; for each bit, double the total and add the bit. For 1011: 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 5 \to 11. It is the chain form from the derivation. "(19)_8" is not an octal numeral, because 9 is not an octal digit. In equations like (43)_x = (y3)_8 this quietly adds the conditions x > 4 and y < 8, and missing them gives wrong counts. Practice Positions to the right of the point continue the pattern: b^{-1}, b^{-2}, … So (0.1)_2 = \tfrac12. A digit is worth digit × b^{\text{position}}, counting positions from 0 on the right. Every digit must be smaller than the base. To read fast, use the chain: multiply by b, add the next digit.
